## Chapter 43: Applying Statistics to Business Applications Through Six Sigma

### Common Challenges When Presenting Statistical Analysis

Here's the first, and perhaps the biggest, challenge Six Sigma specialists face when delivering statistical analysis information: most people don't care. Truly, unless your sponsor is also a Six Sigma specialist, or your leadership committee is well versed in Six Sigma methods, the people you're presenting to don't care which hypothesis test you used, or what your Chi-Square statistic or p-value was. That's not to say business leaders and others don't care about your analysis's conclusions or results, and they certainly care about the project's overall outcomes. But you need to find a way to present your information in a way that connects to what they care about, and that doesn't rely exclusively on statistical concepts and language.

A second challenge is that the overall business team and leaders likely don't have the same understanding of statistical analysis a Six Sigma specialist has. The Six Sigma presenter is then tasked with presenting data when the data's foundation may not be understood. As a Six Sigma specialist, you need to be able to explain why the team chose to go in a certain direction, or how you know a process improved, and not everyone is simply going to take your word that the p-value was appropriate for the decision you made.

A third challenge in presenting your analysis is that you can easily get sidetracked or lose focus because of statistics, without managing to get your business point across. This can happen for one of two reasons. First, if your sponsor or another audience member has knowledge of Six Sigma and statistical analysis, they might start asking statistical questions, rather than business questions. Why did you use the 1-Proportion test? How did you choose the sample size? Do you really think a beta of 0.2 is sufficient, or should you have used a beta of 0.1?

Some statistical questions may well be valid. How did you choose the sample size? That might be something worth covering in a presentation, so the audience understands what assumptions the team made, and what risks were considered acceptable. On the other hand, if you've already done the analysis and made decisions based on sample size and hypothesis testing, then it's a moot point whether the power was set correctly. One way to avoid this kind of detour is to keep a sponsor with Six Sigma knowledge involved throughout the project; that way, they can provide input on such things in real time, if desired.

The other reason you might get lost in statistics when you should be presenting business-relevant information is because your audience doesn't understand the statistics, turning the presentation into a statistics lesson. It's important to find the balance between educating the audience on information needed about the Six Sigma process, and providing an in-depth discussion of statistical analysis. For example, you'd probably want to make sure your audience understands what standard deviation is and why it matters. You probably don't need to explain every type of hypothesis test — or even, in some cases, that you used a hypothesis test at all.

A final challenge in presenting statistical data is the tendency to include too much information or too many examples. You have a boxplot, a bar chart, a pie chart, a hypothesis test, and several calculations based on probability distributions. They all look good to you. They all say something a little different about the data. They should all go in the presentation, right? Wrong — too many ways of illustrating the data overwhelm the audience. It's also likely most people within the business won't notice the nuances in the data that a trained Six Sigma specialist notices, which means, from their perspective, you're simply showing the same data over and over. That's not an effective use of presentation space or meeting time.

### Why Include Any Statistics at All?

Even with all the challenges discussed above, you shouldn't leave statistics out of your presentation entirely. Whether presenting findings at a Measure or Analyze tollgate review, or presenting for final approval of improvements, statistics is what gives your conclusions or results credibility. Working your data into a presentation can be hard, but we've provided a few tips for doing so in the next section.

### Tips for Building Business-Accessible Presentations

If it's important to include statistics for credibility, but many people in your business audience likely won't follow the intricacies of the actual analysis, what do you do? This is actually where some of Six Sigma's statistical process control's biggest benefits come in. If you're working in a genuine Six Sigma environment, then you're never working with just the numbers. Remember, from PART I, that Six Sigma cares more about the business — and its goals and success — than about the data and analysis. In fact, the analysis and data are only relevant to the extent they can be used as a tool for making or measuring improvements to business processes.

Because of that, the Six Sigma team should already be grounded in business terms and phrases. Consider the act of writing the problem statement, which we covered in Chapter 9. The problem statement combines statistical concepts with business goals and needs — and it's a good reference point for anyone presenting Six Sigma information throughout, and after, a DMAIC project. If you're not sure whether something should be included in a presentation, ask yourself: does this relate to the problem statement, or to a solution for the problem statement? If not, it's probably not necessary to communicate or present it in a general business setting. As you work with data and statistics, you might be surprised how much your interest in the numbers grows. Although interest in the numbers can lead to valuable findings and conclusions, you need to avoid the temptation to include data or conclusions in a presentation simply because you find them interesting or "cool."

Other ways to build workable business presentations, when dealing with statistics and analysis, include tailoring the presentation to the audience, building a story-style narrative, keeping things short and simple, integrating appropriate images, and avoiding the misuse of technology, presentation, or statistical tools.

**Understand the Target Audience**

When presenting or communicating about a Six Sigma project or statistical analysis, tailor the information to reflect your audience's level of concern and knowledge. For example, consider a Six Sigma Black Belt presenting at an Improve tollgate review meeting. The Black Belt is presenting to a leadership team, which includes the project sponsor. At least two members of the leadership team are also Black Belts — maybe one is even a Master Black Belt.

Given that scenario, the audience is both invested in the information and able to understand many of the statistical concepts behind the decisions the Six Sigma team made during the project. That doesn't mean you should automatically include all your data in the presentation — your audience is busy too. But it does mean you should anticipate at least a few questions about methodology or statistical analysis, and you can work some technical terms or results into your presentation without worrying about needing to explain them.

When dealing with this kind of audience, it's generally a good idea to build a presentation appendix. You can put your analysis, data tables, and even specific Minitab results in the appendix, where they can be quickly pulled up if a specific question calls for it. In situations involving high costs or high risks, leadership teams are more likely to want to see the underlying analysis, because they need to fully understand every assumption and risk, before deciding on the recommended improvements.

In other situations, you might be called on to present Six Sigma information or statistical findings to less-invested audiences, or ones with no statistics background at all. Examples include presenting to general management, or presenting the reasons behind changes to the team of a department impacted by a Six Sigma process improvement. When that happens, it can help to rely on graphical representations of your analysis, particularly if the information you're trying to share is very evident in a certain type of chart.

For example, a Six Sigma team at a government agency was tasked with improving output for a workflow process that involves reviewing financial assistance applications. The team made improvements to the process and now compares the process's average hourly production rate before the changes to the current average rate. To do this, they run a 2-Sample T-Test, to determine whether the new data has a higher mean than the old data. The Minitab results are presented below.

```
Two-Sample T-Test and CI: C1, C2

Two-sample T for C1 vs C2

     N  Mean  StDev  SE Mean
C1  23  4.00   2.76     0.58
C2  23  6.35   3.11     0.65

Difference = μ (C1) - μ (C2)
Estimate for difference:  -2.348
95% upper bound for difference:  -0.889
T-Test of difference = 0 (vs <): T-Value = -2.70  P-Value = 0.005  DF = 43

```

Knowing what you know about hypothesis testing and p-values, you can quickly see that we reject the null hypothesis and accept the alternative. Yes, the process means changed. According to our statistical analysis, it's a more productive process.

But can you just copy this data from Minitab onto a PowerPoint slide? Probably not — only a Six Sigma or statistical analysis specialist would be able to make that connection between the p-value and the real-world conclusion.

Consider the graphical image below.

<img alt="Boxplot genérico comparando C1 e C2" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


This is a boxplot of the same data used to build the 2-Sample T-Test above, but it provides a more business-friendly version of the data for most business employees. You can quickly see that process C2 has a higher production rate than process C1 — even if you don't know anything about boxplots.

It's not enough to understand how the target audience is likely to interact with the data and statistical analysis. When building a presentation about your project or statistical data, you also need to understand what the target audience wants to know, and how they need to know it.

- High-level leadership typically wants to know whether the project was a success, how you know it was a success, what savings or gains can be expected, and how you're controlling the process to make sure the same problems don't come back.
- Process owners and employees close to the process should know all of that, though you may need to widen the discussions about costs and savings, to leave out sensitive data that might be included in an executive-level presentation (like assumptions about employee compensation). Process owners and employees are also likely to want more detail about the specific process changes — why those changes were implemented, and how they impact day-to-day workflow? Where leadership might be satisfied with a high-level process map, for example, process owners want to see more granular maps.
- Audience members from different departments will likely ask questions that make sense from their perspective, so know who'll be in a tollgate meeting or other type of presentation, and be prepared to answer questions specific to their world.
- The compliance team asks about adherence to regulations. Did the team consider regulations when making decisions? What happens when compliance required a decision that seemed to run opposite to what the statistical inferences indicated to the team? Did the team calculate the risks and costs associated with compliance failures, which are often bigger than other process failures?
- The accounting or finance team asks about budget, revenue, and savings. Does the team have a chart that shows results in dollar-value form? What's the likelihood of saving above a certain amount? Can the team tie a dollar value to various analyses, changes, or improvements?
- The marketing, sales, and customer service team is likely to ask about customer-facing and customer-centered information. How did the team collect the voice of the customer? What assumptions about the customer did the team make? When making process changes or analyzing data, how did the team factor in the customer?

You obviously can't build a presentation that answers every possible question about your process, project, or statistical analysis. The presentation would be huge and would take too long to deliver. It's generally a good idea to keep a presentation under 10 to 20 minutes, with plenty of time for questions, and your presentation time may be even more limited, depending on organizational business practices. So, you should always answer the biggest, most important questions about your improvements, project, or DMAIC step in the presentation, and be prepared for other types of questions in the Q&A session (this is where an appendix can help).

### Tell a Story With Text and Images

Use PowerPoint or another presentation program, to combine your information in a way that tells a story the audience can understand and care about. Keeping your audience and your presentation's purpose in mind, try to tell an overall story throughout the whole presentation, while presenting "mini-narratives" on each slide.

Consider the example slide below, which presents the 2-Sample T-Test information we used earlier in this chapter. The slide tells a story through the placement of information, the inclusion of a chart, and a question-and-answer format. This is an easy template, one that can be used on most Six Sigma presentation slides, particularly when presenting statistical analysis or data.

<img alt="Slide de exemplo: "Did changes improve hourly production rates?" com boxplot, hipóteses nula/alternativa, teste usado, valor-p, e conclusão" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


- First, phrase a question as the slide's title. Make it a concise question, but try to write a question that stands on its own. The example slide doesn't do a great job of this: which changes, which process, and which hourly rates are being discussed? Within the context of a whole presentation, that isn't a problem. However, you may want to pull a single slide for an email communication or training document — and executive leaders tend to pull a single slide or graphical image, to communicate information about a sponsored project. A better title for this slide might be "Did the software changes to the Assistance Application Review workflow increase hourly production rates?"
- Next, include an image that answers your question, or provides additional information about the data or process. Images, charts, and maps break up long blocks of text in a presentation, making it easier for the audience to digest. By presenting data in a variety of formats on a slide, you also capture the interest and understanding of a broader audience. Graphical representations of the data often get the point across faster, and can help you tell a complex data story in a short amount of time.
- It may be a good idea to include some basic statistical information, like a business-accessible version of the null and alternative hypothesis. At minimum, everyone in the audience can understand that these two statements are what the team was evaluating, and only one of them can be true. Including the type of test run and the p-value is optional, but can be a good idea, both for the team's own reference and to inform sponsors or others who also have Six Sigma knowledge.
- Finally, answer the question asked in the title, with a short, text-based conclusion. The conclusion should align with any graphical representation or statistical test data included on the slide. You should avoid presenting contradictory data and conclusions on a single slide, unless you have a specific reason to do so, and an explanation of why the contradiction matters.

Not every question requires every element of the slide above. Sometimes, it makes sense to provide the answer in concise text. For example, you might ask "What problem is the team trying to solve?" The right content for that slide would be the problem statement, as written during the Define phase.

Sometimes, the only thing you need to include on the slide is a chart. Consider the slide below.

<img alt="Slide de exemplo: "What is causing defective orders?" com um gráfico de Pareto dos tipos de erro" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


This slide asks what's causing defective orders, and answers the question with a Pareto chart. Even if someone isn't familiar with the Pareto chart, it's pretty obvious, given the labels and data, that the issue creating the most defects is in the product's finishing. Someone who knows Pareto charts could see, within seconds, that finishing errors and defective raw materials account for over 60% of the errors; add "wrong product selected," and that accounts for 80% of the errors.

Some Six Sigma tools, like the Pareto chart, are easy to explain to audience members who have no prior understanding of data analysis or Six Sigma. Given a minute or two of presentation time, you could sufficiently explain how the chart above answers the slide's question, and that's one reason Pareto charts (and other bar-type charts) are popular in such presentations.

### Be Clear and Concise

No matter how you're presenting your data, make sure every slide — and every element on the slide — is clear and concise. That means writing in active language as much as possible, avoiding long text explanations, and making sure everything is written correctly, and that you didn't accidentally use the wrong word. When including statistics in a presentation, it's easy to make an incorrect word choice that changes the meaning of your entire statement. Simply saying "greater than" when you meant "less than," or "decrease" when you meant "increase," can distort the information you're providing, or make it confusing for your audience.

Clarity isn't just a concern in word choice and sentence structure. You should also worry about how the elements on your slide combine. Don't put so much information on a single slide that words or images become unintelligible to the audience. In some cases, you may need to ask a question and answer it across a series of slides.

Be aware that a projected slide's image is never as clear as the image on your computer. Because of that, you should always avoid overlaying light-colored font or images on a light background, or dark-colored font or images on a dark background. Don't shrink fonts down to something as small as 12 points, just to fit all the information — remember, your audience may be sitting yards or dozens of yards away. You also don't need to include every last piece of information on a slide — the slide should serve as the audience's visual reference point, while you add information verbally.

The text and images you add directly to the slide shouldn't be your only concern. You also need to make sure the text and images inside your charts are as clear and concise as possible. Consider the two boxplots below.

<img alt="Boxplot genérico C1, C2, sem rótulos descritivos" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


The first boxplot, by itself, doesn't provide much information for an audience. Someone who understands boxplots could only tell that two things were being represented, and that one's mean was higher than the other's.

<img alt="Boxplot editado com título "Average Production Per Hour for Application Workflow" e rótulos "OldProcess"/"NewProcess"" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />


The second boxplot is the same as the first, but the title and data labels have been edited. Now you can see the chart provides information about the application workflow. Specifically, the chart is illustrating the average hourly production rates for that workflow, and the new workflow process appears more productive than the old one.

Building graphical analyses that tell a small story on their own — with the help of data labels and titles — matters. First, as the Six Sigma presenter, the labels provide cues that help you verbally explain the slide or chart. After several slides with similarly looking charts, even you can get confused about which specific data you're discussing. Second, proper labeling on such images lets you reuse the image, without the presentation's or slide's context. That means you waste less time, and can reuse your work when communicating about your project or data — effectively reducing rework muda. Finally, you don't need to worry as much about someone taking your data or analysis and misreading it, or drawing the wrong idea from it. If the charts are properly labeled, it's harder for someone viewing the information outside your presentation to draw the wrong conclusions.

You can also edit the data colors in charts, in both Minitab and Excel, making it even easier for an audience to draw appropriate conclusions from the illustration. Consider the Pareto chart below. This is the same Pareto chart shown earlier in this chapter, but, in this version, the top three categories are presented in red. The color change emphasizes those categories, which account for 80% of the errors, making it easier for the audience to draw the conclusion that these are the issues the team will focus on.

<img alt="Gráfico de Pareto de Tipos de Erro, com as três principais categorias destacadas em vermelho e as demais em azul" src="data:image/png;base64," style="max-width:700px;width:100%;height:auto;display:block;margin:0.6rem auto;"  />

### Don't Misuse Your Tools

One final tip for building business-accessible presentations: don't misuse the tools, knowledge, and resources you have for building presentations or communicating ideas.

Don't misuse PowerPoint, for example. Most audience members don't want to see a 100-slide presentation. Just because you can include something doesn't mean you should. Likewise, try to avoid animating every aspect of your presentation. Yes, there's a time for a fade-in or fly-in, but the time isn't for every bullet point or image. Use animations sparingly — if you use them at all — to give impact to conclusions or very important elements of your presentation. For the most part, a strong Six Sigma presentation should rely on clarity and data, rather than tricks and animations.

Don't misuse Minitab or any other statistical analysis software you have. It takes mere seconds to run certain tests or build charts in Minitab, as you'll see in the next Unit. Because of that, Six Sigma analysts and teams tend to pile up many versions of data. Treat Minitab charts and analyses the way you treat PowerPoint animations. Use them as needed, but don't use them just because they're available. A good rule is no more than one chart per slide or per data-related question. That forces you to pick the chart you feel most powerfully or appropriately illustrates your data. There are exceptions to this rule, and you may need to include two charts, if one helps explain the other, or if you're comparing information about data or multiple data sets.

Don't misuse your data analysis skills. Misuse of data analysis can come in one of two forms: either you inadvertently make a data analysis mistake, or you force an analysis to fit a desired outcome or conclusion. The first is more of an error than a misuse; you can avoid presenting such mistakes to others by double-checking every conclusion and inference, and having someone else with Six Sigma knowledge review your analysis, before finalizing a presentation. That's why many Six Sigma organizations have at least one Master Black Belt on staff — Black Belts and Green Belts can turn to the Master Black Belt if they have analysis questions, or simply want to confirm they're on the right track with the analysis.

No one is infallible, and mistakes can happen. As a Six Sigma specialist, though, you can never let bias force statistical conclusions that aren't backed by the data. And you should certainly never obscure an analysis, presenting it in a way that makes it hard for your audience to see the appropriate conclusion, because you want them to draw a different one. For example, the trick used above, to highlight a certain part of the Pareto chart with color, can be misused. You can draw attention to a certain part of a chart or bar chart with color, increasing the chance the audience will conclude the colored portion is more relevant or more important than the chart's other data. Although that's sometimes true, Six Sigma teams and presenters need to be careful using such tactics — only create that scenario when the data supports that emphasis.

Another example of building bias into a presentation happens when you present analysis information knowing the sample size wasn't large enough for solid conclusions, but you don't make that clear when presenting the information. That can result in leadership or others making decisions based on your data, without understanding the risks that the conclusions could be wrong.

Similarly, if you run four types of tests in Minitab, and three support one conclusion, while only a single test supports the conclusion the team originally wanted to present, you shouldn't present only the single test's results. Before presenting anything, you should review each of the tests, to understand why one of them differs; you should also make sure the tests you're using are appropriate for the data, the question, and the sample size at hand. If you verify the statistics are all correct, then you generally go with the conclusion supported by the greater number of tests.

### Don't Let the Presentation Drive the Project

Given the decision-making processes and requirements in the corporate world, presentations are a requirement of the DMAIC process. Six Sigma teams and specialists will have to present their findings at some point, so presentation skills are something you genuinely need to work on.

That said, it's important that you never let the need for a good presentation drive any part of the process. Six Sigma teams should never make decisions about data collection, graphical analysis, process mapping, brainstorming, or any other Six Sigma function, because they think it'll look good or look nice for the presentation. Instead, presenting information to the business needs to come after the work is done.

That truth is relevant whenever you're presenting information to the business or the business team — not just when you're standing in front of a conference room, with a PowerPoint behind you. For example, Black Belts often communicate with sponsors or business leaders regularly, throughout a DMAIC project. Maybe the team provides a daily email or a weekly update to the sponsor; whatever the communication mode, every tip in this chapter is relevant.
